inhalt: Addressing consumption is a central part of reducing climate impact from the volume of new products purchased to the carbon footprint of how we use these products.

Fashion possesses one of the most powerful marketing engines on earth. Brands, designers, imagemakers and the media have a major influence on the identities, values and actions of billions of people across all segments of society.

The aim is to shift the fashion narrative from one of extraction, exploitation and disposable consumption, towards regeneration, equity and care by increasing consumer awareness, industry accountability and policy breakthroughs.
Every year, 92 million tonnes of textile waste is produced globally. Production doubled from 2000 to 2015, while the duration of garment use decreased by 36 per cent.
Eleven per cent of plastic waste comes from clothing and textiles, with only 8 per cent of textiles fibres in 2023 made from recycled sources.
Unsustainable fashion is aggravating the triple planetary crisis of climate change, nature, land and biodiversity loss, and pollution and waste.
The Ellen Macarthur Foundation, a UNEP partner, has estimated that a truckload of abandoned textiles is dumped in landfill or incinerated every second.

Plastic fibres are polluting the oceans, the wastewater, toxic dyes, and the exploitation of underpaid workers. Fast fashion is big business, and while the environmental costs are rising, experts say there is another way: a circular economy for textiles.

The fast fashion business model of quick turnover, high volume, cheap prices is under pressure from consumers who are demanding change. They want resilient garments from a sustainable industry, a goal supported by the UN Alliance for Sustainable Fashion.
The Sustainable Fashion Communication Playbook provides a practical guide for fashion communicators to contribute to sustainable change by shifting the narrative of the sector.
The International Day of Zero Waste highlights the importance of bolstering waste management globally and rethinking fashion consumption.
Textile and fashion waste in cities often end up in landfills, where it takes decades to decompose and releases harmful greenhouse gases.
A zero-waste approach is key to the required transition to more circular approaches in the fashion and textiles industry.
The United Wardrobe Project transforms textile waste into a cycle of reuse and renewal, cutting CO2 emissions and conserving water.
Textiles-as-a-service models, like leasing repairable garments, foster sustainability and educate new generations on waste reduction.
Pioneering initiatives redirect post-consumer textiles from landfills to markets via textile recovery facilities to close the loop.

The EU has a Strategy for Sustainable and Circular Textiles to create a greener textiles sector. The aim is a major shift inside the industry and among consumers, creating a whole new sustainable ecosystem for textiles by the end of this decade.
titel: How the EU is making fashion sustainable

inhalt: The new approach looks at the entire lifecycle of textiles and proposes actions to change the way we produce and consume textiles. It means that all textile products must be durable, repairable and recyclable.

inhalt: Did you know that 80% of a product’s environment footprint throughout its life cycle is determined when it is designed? This is why the EU will set new design requirements for textiles to make them last longer, easier to repair and recycle.

inhalt: The textiles industry is a major user of hazardous chemicals and industrial polluter of freshwater worldwide. Some chemicals are known to cause cancer or disrupt hormonal systems.
Washing clothes made of synthetic fibres releases microplastic fibres into waterways. PFCs used for waterproofing are released into the atmosphere and found in remote regions.
Less than half of used clothes are collected for reuse or recycling when they are no longer wanted and only 1% are recycled into new clothes.
Textile-to-textile recycling is still a big technical challenge, also because most garments are made of mixed fabrics and are therefore difficult or impossible to recycle at all.
Production in the supply chain has the largest carbon footprint, with estimates varying between 3 - 10% of global GHG emissions.
Cotton is grown on only 2.4% of the world’s cultivated land but uses 6% of the world’s pesticides and 16% of insecticides, degrading the land.
The destruction of unsold goods is one of the most shocking consequences of overproduction. For many brands, destruction of unsold stock is still standard practice.
Dyeing and finishing (wet processing) is responsible for 36% of GHG emissions, followed by fibre preparation (spinning) at 28%.
The rise of fast fashion has led to consumers seeing cheap clothes more and more as 'perishable goods' that are worn a few times and then thrown away.
Regulators must finally take responsibility for changing the way that fashion is made. Business as usual cannot continue, and practices that devastate the planet must be regulated.
The fashion industry must transition to a model that respects planetary boundaries and ensures social justice for workers.
Hazardous chemicals used in textile production can persist in the environment and bioaccumulate in the food chain.
The 'take-make-waste' model of the fashion industry is fundamentally incompatible with a sustainable future.
Slowing down fashion means producing fewer, higher-quality garments that are designed to last for years, not weeks.
Microplastic pollution from synthetic textiles is a global environmental threat that requires urgent action at the source.
Regenerative fashion models aim to restore ecosystems and support local communities rather than just minimizing harm.
The fashion industry must be held responsible for the entire lifecycle of its products, including end-of-life management.
True sustainability in fashion requires a fundamental rethink of our relationship with clothing and consumption.
The fashion industry is a major contributor to global water scarcity and pollution, especially in production regions.
The use of toxic dyes in the fashion industry has devastating impacts on the health of workers and local ecosystems.
Fast fashion brands often use vague sustainability claims to distract from their overall environmental impact.
The fashion industry must move away from the constant pressure for growth and embrace a steady-state economy model.
Sustainable fashion is not just about materials; it's about changing the entire system of production and consumption.
The fashion industry's impact on biodiversity is often overlooked but is significant due to land use and pollution.
We need a global treaty on plastic pollution that includes specific measures to address microplastics from textiles.
The fashion industry must ensure that the transition to sustainability is just and inclusive for all workers in the supply chain.
The rise of ultra-fast fashion brands has further accelerated the environmental and social crisis of the industry.
Sustainable fashion requires a long-term perspective that values durability and timeless design over fleeting trends.
The fashion industry must be transparent about its chemical use and commit to a zero-discharge policy for hazardous substances.
The environmental cost of fashion is often hidden from consumers, leading to a lack of awareness about the true impact of their purchases.
The fashion industry must embrace a culture of care and repair to extend the life of garments and reduce waste.
The transition to sustainable fashion is an urgent necessity to protect the planet and ensure a livable future for all.
The fashion industry has the potential to be a force for good if it embraces sustainability and social responsibility.
The fashion industry must be held accountable for its role in the global climate and environmental emergency.
Sustainable fashion is a journey that requires continuous improvement and collaboration across the entire industry.
The fashion industry must listen to the voices of those most affected by its negative impacts and work towards a more equitable future.
The future of fashion depends on our ability to transform the industry into one that is truly sustainable and ethical.
The fashion industry must act now to reduce its environmental footprint and protect the planet for future generations.
